verses.1: Al-Mizan reports that some exegetes identify the town as Mecca, corroborated by the chapter’s Meccan theme and its connection with the father of (90:3). It explains the repeated town and the Prophet’s ḥill as honoring Mecca through his residence or birthplace, and allows a parenthetical reading. It reports al-Kashshāf’s alternatives: ḥill may mean that the Prophet’s ḥurmah is violated, rebuking Meccan persecution and strengthening him, or that he will conquer Mecca and be unrestricted there. Both derive ḥill from ḥall as muḥill, the opposite of muḥrim, meaning that the sanctuary’s restrictions will temporarily be lifted for him.

verses.3: Al-Mizan regards Abraham and Ishmael as the clearest father and son, because the oaths should cohere with Mecca: they raised the Holy House (2:127), and Abraham prayed that the city be a sanctuary (14:35). Thus the thread swears by Mecca, its resident Prophet, and its founders. It rejects the unrestricted Abrahamic progeny reading because it would include idolaters such as Abū Lahab and Abū Jahl; if extended to progeny, it must be confined to believers. It says the Adam-and-all-progeny reading is sound in itself but fails to connect with the preceding Meccan oaths, and judges the other proposals far from the text.
verses.4: Al-Mizan takes kabad as toil and exhaustion and this verse as the oaths’ main conclusion. Human life is enveloped by hardship: even sought-after worldly pleasures are mixed with struggle and suffering, while unforeseen tragedies and natural disasters also overtake people.
verses.5: Al-Mizan argues that humanity’s inescapable travail shows it is subject to a higher power: God overrides desires, limits plans, manages people as He wills, and may seize them in punishment. Imagining independence can lead to sin, arrogant refusal of service, self-congratulatory spending in God’s way, and ostentation through riyāʾ and sumʿah, as in the boast of (90:6).
verses.6: Al-Mizan defines lubadan as abundant and, from the context, tentatively links the verse to someone who professed or inclined to Islam, gave charity, then boasted of his impressive expenditure. It says God rejects that claim: true felicity requires the difficult undertaking of spending in God’s way through the defile (90:11-16), together with faith and mutual exhortation to patience and mercy (90:17). It says narrations to be examined will confirm this interpretation.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says the boast of immense spending implies that God is unaware of it, whereas God is All-Seeing of the person’s expenditure. That sacrifice is insufficient for true felicity; the person must bear a more taxing servitude by taking the narrow pass, joining believers, and acquiring their virtues (90:11-17).
verses.8: Al-Mizan says eyes enable knowledge of visible things, while tongue and lips enable speech, communication of inward knowledge, and learning beyond sight. Al-najdayn are the uphill paths of good and evil, so called because each requires effort; it rejects the two-breasts reading. God’s endowment of human sight, speech, and moral discernment supports the conclusion that He sees deeds, knows intentions, and distinguishes good from evil.

verses.11: Al-Mizan defines iqtiḥām as forceful, laborious undertaking and ʿaqabah as a difficult, rugged steep incline. Venturing the defile means making a charitable expenditure that is difficult for its donor, as the following verses explain; it rejects the claim that the verse curses the speaker of (90:6).
verses.12: Al-Mizan says the question magnifies al-ʿaqabah, the arduous defile. The defile itself is fakk, freeing a slave, with an omitted feminine hiya referring to ʿaqabah; it rejects a more contrived masculine syntactic account. It includes feeding in famine an orphaned relative or a destitute person bound to the dust: masghabah is starvation, maqrabah blood relation, and matrabah extreme destitution. These acts exemplify mercy, with liberation mentioned first for Islam’s special concern for freeing slaves, and must be joined to faith and mutual exhortation to obedience, patience, and compassion.

verses.18: Al-Mizan takes al-maymanah as yumn—felicity, blessing, and auspiciousness—the opposite of shuʾm. It identifies these people as those who undertake the defile, believe, and urge patience and compassion, whose faith and deeds bring bliss and blessings. It rejects the alternative of the right side, because that does not fit the contrast with al-mashʾamah.
verses.19: Al-Mizan takes God’s signs without restriction: creational signs in the horizons and souls, the Qur’an, and all teachings revealed and propagated by His messengers. They establish God’s absolute oneness as Lord and object of worship; defying them is defying God, kufr. Al-mashʾamah means misery, misfortune, and inauspiciousness, the opposite of al-maymanah, and its people are enclosed in a muʾṣadah fire, locked and shut.
